analysis.one_liner: Bans toxic flame retardant chemicals from the filling material in children's cushioned products.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban flame retardants from children's products was referred to a House committee in 2013 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat any children's cushioned product — strollers, car seats, bassinets, changing pads, infant mattresses and similar items — as a banned hazardous substance if its filling material contains more than 1,000 parts per million of organohalogen or organophosphorous flame retardant chemicals, starting one year after passage. The bill's findings cite research linking these chemicals to cancer, hormone disruption, reduced IQ, and developmental harm, and note that studies show no measurable fire-safety benefit from these chemicals in such products. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Babies and young children, who are exposed to flame retardants mainly by ingesting contaminated household dust as they crawl and play on floors, and their parents. The bill's findings state that U.S. children have among the highest body levels of these chemicals in the world, with toddlers showing three times the blood levels of their mothers, and that the chemicals are associated with cancer, endocrine disruption, reduced IQ, and birth defects. It would also simplify shopping: parents could buy a car seat or nursing pillow without a toxic-chemical risk the bill says provides no real fire protection.

how_it_helps.text: Bans organohalogen and organophosphorous flame retardants in the resilient filling of children's cushioned products above 1,000 ppm by weight, treating such products as banned hazardous substances under the Federal Hazardous Substances Act.

The bill's findings state that over 80 percent of children's cushioned products tested in a 2011 study contained at least one flame retardant chemical, and that these chemicals are associated with cancer, endocrine and immune disruption, reduced IQ, reduced fertility, and birth defects.

The findings say the chemicals provide no measurable fire safety benefit in these products: children's cushioned items contain little filling material and California had already exempted strollers, infant carriers, and nursing pillows from its flammability standard as not presenting a significant fire hazard.

The bill covers a broad list of products children use daily, including car seats, strollers, bassinets, infant swings, changing pads, floor play mats, and infant mattresses, with a compliance date one year after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Flame retardant chemical manufacturers, whose organohalogen and organophosphorous products would lose a market in children's goods, and children's product makers, who would need to reformulate filling materials and certify compliance within a year. Those compliance costs would likely be passed through to consumers in product prices, though only modestly since the chemicals themselves add cost and were already being phased out under California's revised flammability standard, which many manufacturers follow nationwide.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would face a one-year deadline to reformulate and certify products, a cost that would be passed to consumers in the price of car seats, strollers, and other baby gear.

A bright-line 1,000 ppm ban is a blunt instrument: it covers every organohalogen and organophosphorous compound regardless of the toxicology of the specific chemical, so a less hazardous compound would be treated the same as a well-documented one.
With 6 members of the House behind it and no committee action, the bill was never debated or improved through the normal process, so any design flaws were never examined in public hearings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are significant and one-sided: the bill targets chemicals that children absorb through household dust, that the bill's own findings say add no measurable fire protection in these products, and that states like California were already moving to exempt from flammability requirements. The costs are real but routine for product regulation — reformulation costs for manufacturers, likely passed to parents in modestly higher prices. The 1,000 ppm bright line is less flexible than a chemical-by-chemical safety review, but it is far faster, and speed matters when the exposure is children. On balance, the benefits outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Decrease Unsafe Toxins Act on August 1, 2013, joined by five Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade.
No further action was taken: no hearing was held, no vote occurred, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Flame retardant chemical makers and product manufacturers benefit from the bill's death, since no federal ban on the chemicals was enacted. Parents and young children lost the protection the bill would have provided; the chemicals remained legal in children's products.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Flame retardant chemical makers; parents and children lost

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks in the House.

for.name: Reps. Barbara Lee, Gwen Moore, Louise Slaughter, Charles Rangel, and Grace Meng

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, never held a hearing, never reported it out, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, House Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral the day after introduction and took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters were House Democrats; the bill received no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would bar organohalogen and organophosphorous flame retardants above 1,000 ppm in the filling of children's cushioned products, removing a market for these chemicals. The bill's findings say the chemicals carry health risks and provide no fire-safety benefit in these products.

industries.industry: Children's product manufacturers (strollers, car seats, bassinets, infant mattresses)
industries.note: Manufacturers would bear reformulation and compliance costs within one year, but California was already revising its flammability standard to exempt many baby products, so many were headed in this direction anyway. A uniform federal rule also simplifies compliance versus a patchwork of state standards.
